title: Global Entanglement Quantification via Classical Shadows
authors: João P. Engster, Eduardo I. Duzzioni
abstract: Detecting and characterizing quantum correlations are tasks of great relevance in quantum information. More specifically, quantifying the amount of multipartite entanglement is a known difficult task, even for pure states. To this end, several entanglement measures have been proposed, although there is currently no universal manner to do so. In this work, we propose the classical shadows technique to measure the generalized global entanglement introduced in Phys. Rev. A 74, 022314. This particular multipartite entanglement quantifier $E_G^{(n)}$ relies on the linear entropies of all $n$-qubit partitions of a state. As the linear entropy can be written in terms of a complete set of observables of the subsystem, we employ classical shadows to estimate many observables with fewer measurements. We simulate the quantification of $E_G^{(n)}$ for well-known entangled states and for random states, comparing shadow estimations and grouping techniques. Our results show a clear advantage of classical shadows over direct estimation approaches, indicating that it can be a useful tool to quantify entanglement without the need to reconstruct the density operator of the whole system.
summary: This paper introduces the use of the classical shadows technique to estimate the generalized global entanglement, $E_G^{(n)}$, which quantifies multipartite entanglement. By leveraging classical shadows, the authors overcome the severe measurement overhead associated with directly estimating all necessary Pauli observables. The results demonstrate that this method offers a clear, resource-efficient advantage over traditional estimation techniques for characterizing entanglement in large quantum systems.
main_problem: The core challenge is quantifying multipartite entanglement, a difficult task for which no universal measure exists.
main_result: The classical shadows technique provides a significant and measurable advantage over direct estimation methods for quantifying global entanglement, especially for large systems with limited measurement resources.
method: The authors propose using the classical shadows protocol to estimate the expectation values of Pauli observables required for the generalized global entanglement measure, $E_G^{(n)}$.
model_or_system: The study analyzes general quantum states ($ho$) across $n$-qubit partitions, simulating results for well-known entangled states like GHZ, W, and EPR states, as well as random states.
key_observables: Generalized global entanglement ($E_G^{(n)}$), linear entropy of reduced density matrices ($	ext{SL}(ho_{\ell})$), and expectation values of Pauli observables.
important_parameters: The analysis explores scaling with system size ($N$), the number of qubits in the partition ($n$), and measurement resource ratios ($r$).
main_assumptions: The classical shadows estimator is only unbiased in the asymptotic limit, and direct estimation suffers from severe scaling issues.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the faster convergence of shadow estimations towards the exact entanglement value compared to grouping methods, particularly as system size or required observables increase.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the entanglement measure, details the classical shadows technique for estimating required observables, compares its performance against grouping methods (QWC, FC) through simulations on various entangled states, and concludes with a demonstration of its feasibility in resource-limited regimes.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial resource-efficient tool for characterizing complex quantum correlations, which is vital for benchmarking quantum hardware and understanding entanglement scaling in many-body quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. E(2) G as a function of the total number of measure- ments for 10-qubit GHZ, EPR, W, and random states, re- quiring the estimation of 675 Pauli words. The results show a faster convergence to the exact entanglement value (dotted line) for shadow estimations, and the insets highlight how, even with different values of r, the randomized shadow esti- mations perform as well as the derandomized shadow proto- col. The uncertainty bars represent the standard deviation over ten independent runs.

FIG. 3. Absolute difference between the exact and estimated values of E(2) G for different system sizes, considering GHZ, EPR, W, and Haar random states. When the system size grows, the absolute error estimated with grouping methods also grows, while the shadow approach is able to maintain the errors relatively low.

FIG. 2. E(3) G as a function of the total number of measure- ments for 10-qubit GHZ, EPR, W, and random states. The results strengthen the observations in Fig 1, tackling a signif- icantly harder estimation task, involving 7560 observables to characterize E(3) G . The uncertainty bars represent the stan- dard deviation over ten independent runs.
